units.title: Unit 69 — Greetings, farewells and special expressions
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 69. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Greet people naturally in formal and informal first meetings and everyday encounters.
Ask how someone is and answer with common follow-up expressions.
Choose suitable informal and polite farewells, including weekend wishes and their replies.
Respond appropriately to congratulations, good wishes, relief, toasts, and sneezing.
Describe basic greeting customs using introduced to, shake hands, greet, and cheek.

items.example: I was introduced to our new colleague before the meeting.
items.note: A first meeting can begin when another person tells you someone’s name.

items.example: She asked a stranger for directions to the station.
items.note: Someone you have never met before; not necessarily an unfriendly person.

items.example: In a formal situation, people may introduce themselves by their full names.
items.note: Contrast a formal first meeting with an informal conversation with friends.

items.pt: apertar as mãos; cumprimentar com um aperto de mão
items.example: We shook hands when we met for the first time.
items.note: A conventional greeting in some settings; past: shook hands.

items.example: How do people usually greet friends in your country?
items.note: Greet means welcome or say hello to someone.

items.pt: em uma bochecha; em um dos lados do rosto
items.example: Some people kiss friends on one cheek when they meet.
items.note: Cheek means one side of the face; customs vary among people and cultures.

items.example: They kissed each other on both cheeks at the reunion.
items.note: Both cheeks means the two sides of the face; greeting customs are not universal.

items.example: Hello! I’m here to see Mr Hall.
items.note: A neutral greeting that works in formal and informal situations.

items.example: Hi! It’s good to see you again.
items.note: Informal greeting, especially among friends.

items.example: Nice to meet you, Anna. I’ve heard a lot about your work.
items.note: Said when meeting someone for the first time; also suitable when saying goodbye soon afterwards.

items.example: How are you? You look much happier today.
items.note: A standard friendly greeting that normally invites a brief response.

items.example: Fine, thanks. I had a relaxing weekend.
items.note: A common short answer to How are you?

items.example: I’m doing well, thanks. How about you?
items.note: Returns a greeting question to the other person.

items.pt: como vão as coisas?; e aí, tudo bem?
items.example: How’s it going? Have you settled into your new flat?
items.note: Informal way to ask how someone is or how things are progressing.

items.example: How are things? Is work any less busy now?
items.note: Informal general greeting about someone’s life.

items.example: Not bad, thanks. The week has been quite good.
items.note: Common understated response; it normally means reasonably well.

items.pt: até que bem, obrigado(a); nada mal
items.example: Not so bad, thanks. And how are you?
items.note: An alternative short answer to How are things?; informal.

items.example: I’m fine, thank you. And you?
items.note: Another brief way to ask the other person the same question.

items.example: Goodbye, Mrs Price. It was a pleasure meeting you.
items.note: Suitable for formal or neutral partings.

items.example: Bye! I’ll call you tonight.
items.note: Short, informal form of goodbye.

items.example: Cheers, everyone. See you next week.
items.note: Informal British English farewell; a separate sense from cheers said during a toast.

items.example: Take care, and give my regards to your family.
items.note: Warm, informal way to say goodbye.

items.example: See you later. I should be back after lunch.
items.note: A casual farewell; see you soon/tomorrow are related variants.

items.example: See you tomorrow. The class starts at nine.
items.note: Farewell used when you expect to meet the person the following day.

items.pt: tenha um bom fim de semana
items.example: Have a nice weekend! Enjoy your time at the coast.
items.note: Common Friday farewell to a colleague, classmate or acquaintance.

items.example: Have a lovely weekend! Same to you!
items.note: Reply to a wish; say same to you, not same for you.

items.example: Excuse me, I need to get off at the next stop.
items.note: Polite way to attract attention or ask to move past someone.

items.pt: posso passar, por favor?; você poderia me dar licença?
items.example: Could I just get past? This is my stop.
items.note: A polite request to move through a crowded space; could softens the request.

items.example: Yes, of course. There’s plenty of room for you to pass.
items.note: Friendly affirmative reply to a polite request.

items.example: Good luck with your interview this afternoon!
items.note: Say this before an exam, interview or other event with an uncertain outcome.

items.example: Good luck with the exam! Thanks, I’ll need it.
items.note: Friendly reply to a good-luck wish, especially when the task seems difficult.

items.example: Cheers! Here’s to another great year together.
items.note: Said when raising drinks together; distinct from informal cheers meaning goodbye.

items.example: Thank goodness! Nobody was injured in the storm.
items.note: Expresses relief because something bad did not happen.

items.example: Thank God! We managed to find the lost dog.
items.note: Informal expression of relief; some people prefer not to use religious wording.

items.example: Goodness! Is it nearly midnight already?
items.note: Goodness alone often expresses surprise; different from the relief phrase thank goodness.

items.example: Congratulations on passing your driving test!
items.note: Used to praise or celebrate another person’s success.

items.example: Bless you! That was a very loud sneeze.
items.note: Conventional response when someone sneezes.

units.title: Unit 70 — Prefixes: changing meaning
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 70. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Word formation: negative and other prefixes
learningObjectives: Form negative adjectives with un-, dis-, in-, im-, ir- and il- where the word allows it.
Recognise the meaning and contextual use of common negative adjectives, including contrasts of likelihood, fairness and ability.
Keep the stress on the base word when pronouncing prefixed adjectives.
Use dis-, un-, over-, mis- and re- with verbs to show reversal, excess, errors and repetition.
Apply the patterns to related negative forms introduced in the exercises without inventing non-standard forms.

items.example: She was unhappy with the way the meeting ended.
items.note: Negative of happy formed with un-; the stress remains on the original stressed syllable.

items.example: It was dishonest to hide the true cost from customers.
items.note: Opposite of honest; dis- forms a negative adjective here.

items.example: It is impossible to finish all the work by lunchtime.
items.note: Opposite of possible; the negative prefix has the form im- before p.

items.example: Two answers on the form were incorrect.
items.note: Opposite of correct; in- is one form of a negative adjective prefix.

items.pt: irregular; que não segue um padrão
items.example: His irregular working hours make planning difficult.
items.note: Opposite of regular; the prefix appears as ir- before r.

items.example: It is illegal to park in front of the emergency exit.
items.note: Opposite of legal; il- is used before l.

items.example: These shoes are uncomfortable after a long walk.
items.note: Opposite of comfortable; the main stress remains on com.

items.example: It is unnecessary to print the whole document.
items.note: Not needed; opposite of necessary.

items.example: The café has an unusual name that is hard to remember.
items.note: Not usual or ordinary; it need not imply something bad.

items.example: We had an unexpected visitor on Sunday afternoon.
items.note: Not anticipated or predicted; opposite of expected.

items.example: The view from the top of the mountain was unbelievable.
items.note: Very surprising, either positively or negatively; stress remains on liev.

items.example: We were unable to open the file without the password.
items.note: Unable to + base verb means not able to; do not say unable of.

items.pt: fora de forma; sem condicionamento físico
items.example: I became unfit after several months without exercise.
items.note: In this context, not physically healthy or fit.

items.example: Our team was unlucky to lose in the last minute.
items.note: Having bad luck; not always due to a lack of skill.

items.pt: improvável que; com pouca chance de
items.example: The train is unlikely to arrive before eight.
items.note: Unlikely to + base verb means something probably will not happen.

items.example: It is unfair to give only some candidates extra time.
items.note: Not fair or equal; can describe treatment, rules and decisions.

items.example: I disagree with the suggested solution to the problem.
items.note: Dis- reverses agree; say disagree with someone or something, not disagree to.

items.example: The sun disappeared behind the clouds.
items.note: Dis- gives the opposite of appear.

items.example: Could you unlock the door before the guests arrive?
items.note: Un- reverses the action of locking something.

items.example: The children got undressed before taking a bath.
items.note: Opposite of get dressed; un- indicates the reverse of the action.

items.pt: desfazer as malas; tirar objetos de uma embalagem
items.example: Let’s unpack our bags before going out for dinner.
items.note: Reverse of pack: take the contents out of a bag, box or suitcase.

items.pt: cobrar mais do que o devido
items.example: The shop overcharged me for two items.
items.note: Over- means too much here; overcharge someone for something.

items.example: I misunderstood the instructions and used the wrong date.
items.note: Mis- means incorrectly; past tense: misunderstood.

items.pt: ouvir errado; entender incorretamente o que foi dito
items.example: I misheard the address because of the noise.
items.note: Mis- means incorrectly; past tense: misheard.

items.example: I need to rewrite the first paragraph of my report.
items.note: Re- means again; past tense: rewrote.

items.example: There was an unpleasant smell in the kitchen.
items.note: Opposite of pleasant; shown in the exercise on word formation.

items.example: It was unkind to laugh at his mistake.
items.note: Opposite of kind; describes behaviour lacking consideration.

items.example: The customers became impatient after waiting for an hour.
items.note: Opposite of patient; negative prefix im- before p.

items.example: These shoes are unsuitable for a long walk in the hills.
items.note: Opposite of suitable; unsuitable for + noun/activity.

items.example: I dislike driving through the city centre at rush hour.
items.note: Opposite of like; followed by a noun or an -ing form.

items.example: Please undo the top button of your coat.
items.note: Reverse an action; can mean unfasten something. Opposite of do up in this exercise.

items.example: That jacket was considered unfashionable a few years ago.
items.note: Opposite of fashionable; describes a style that is not currently popular.

items.example: The old bus service is unreliable during the winter.
items.note: Opposite of reliable; describes someone or something you cannot depend on.

items.example: The receptionist sounded unfriendly on the phone.
items.note: Opposite of friendly; can describe people, expressions or behaviour.

items.example: His desk is untidy, but he can always find his notes.
items.note: Opposite of tidy; describes something not neat or organised.

items.example: Her inability to attend the meeting caused a delay.
items.note: Noun opposite of ability; use inability to + base verb. Do not form unability.

items.example: He seems unsociable, but he is simply shy with new people.
items.note: Opposite of sociable; describes someone who does not enjoy socialising much.
